skill.title: Classify a function as injective, surjective, bijective
needs: Recognise a function and its domain/codomain/range

note: Use the SAME method as the references (they are the lesson so far); change one thing, as usual. The method: Assumes f(a) = f(b) and solves algebraically to show the function is injective. Earlier backups were dropped for doing this instead: Uses arrow diagrams and composite evaluation, including a new not-surjective check, instead of algebraically assuming equal outputs.

steps.title: Assume two inputs give the same output

lines.text: $f$ is injective if $f(a) = f(b)$ forces $a = b$.
Different inputs always give different outputs, so $f$ is injective.

references.final: f(a) = f(b) \Rightarrow a = b \text{, so } f \text{ is injective}

steps.title: Look for another input with the same output

lines.text: $f$ is injective only if $f(a) = f(b)$ forces $a = b$. Set $f(b) = 5$.
Since $b \neq 0$, $b = 6$. Then $f(6) = 36 - 36 + 5 = 5 = f(0)$ with $6 \neq 0$, so $f$ is not injective.

skill.title: Transform a graph
skill.input: f(x) and f(x) + k, f(x + h), kf(x)

note: Use the SAME method as the references (they are the lesson so far); change one thing, as usual. The method: Apply vertical and horizontal shifts to a graph (g(x) - 2, g(x + 3)) and state the effect on the domain. Earlier backups were dropped for doing this instead: Finds a translation vector between points and applies it to a point rather than shifting a graph by g(x) + c or g(x + c).

lines.text: Subtracting 2 from the output lowers every point by 2; the domain stays $-2 \le x \le 2$.
Adding 3 to the input shifts every point 3 units left.
$g$ needs its input between $-2$ and $2$.

references.final: \text{(i) } g(x) - 2 \text{ is } g(x) \text{ down 2; (ii) } g(x+3) \text{ is } g(x) \text{ left 3}

steps.title: Work out the formula for g(x)
Shift the graph of f two units to the right

lines.text: $g(x) = f(x-2)$ moves every point of $f$ two units right, so $(x, y)$ becomes $(x+2, y)$.
Plot these seven points, join them with a smooth curve and label it $g(x)$. Label the first graph $f(x)$.

skill.title: Apply Corollary 1: A diagonal divides a parallelogram into two congruent triangles
skill.output: unknown found, justified by citing Corollary 1
needs: Prove triangles congruent (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS)

note: Use the SAME method as the references (they are the lesson so far); change one thing, as usual. The method: Finds the angles/sides of a parallelogram by applying Corollary 1 that a diagonal splits it into two congruent triangles. Earlier backups were dropped for doing this instead: Finds a triangle's area with Heron's formula, which is a different skill, with Corollary 1 only as the last step.

lines.text: The angles of a triangle add to $180^\circ$.
The diagonal $[AC]$ divides the parallelogram into two congruent triangles, $ABC$ and $CDA$, with $B$ matching $D$.
So the angles at $B$ and $D$ are equal.
The diagonal $[AC]$ divides the parallelogram into congruent triangles $ABC$ and $CDA$, with $C$ matching $A$.
So $|\angle BCA| = |\angle DAC|$.
Each angle is $70^\circ$.
